messages.author: 6c182657d328642f
messages.subject: bat point counts
parts:
Hi all,

I am currently working on fruit bat surveys at known roosting sites using=
point counts.=20
The particular site I am working on is small (<3 hectares) and is surroun=
ded by non habitat (water and housing). The population within this area i=
s enormous with over 10,000 roosting at any given time.=20
The counts just completed were undertaken by walking the boundary of bat =
colony and from certain points (somewhat random) recording all bats seen,=
and also recording the field of view (usually 180 degrees). Six point co=
unts were undertaken.

I analysed the data by treating sample effort as a fraction of 1. i.e 180=
degrees is 0.5, and 90 degrees is 0.25. A 360 field of view is required =
to be 1. I did not use the sampling fraction option as fraction varied be=
tween points.=20
Bats are generally not seen beyond 50m, with an ESW of 30m. Interesting d=
etections show a logistic type curve (hazard cosine), increasing from 0, =
peaking at 15m, and declining to close to 0 by 30m. That may indicate bat=
s moved away from the observer, but Distance is robust (?) I think to thi=
s provided animals move no more than detection shoulder (i.e 15-20m)=20
I had some issues with all points being a fraction of 360 degrees and tha=
t all points occurred on outside of colony looking in. But perhaps there =
is no issue there?

My idea would be to establish random points within all potential habitats=
and each point surveyed each year for bats regardless of bats being ther=
e. This would inflate estimate of variance however. Points on edge of hab=
itat may be only 180 degrees but most points are 360 as points lie inside=
colony.=20
Just wondered what others thought.=20

Cheers

--

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: bat point counts
parts:
Brett:

I presume you are detecting bats in flight, not at rest. You don't
state how long your counts last; are they snapshots? If they aren't
snapshots then you are at risk of animals moving into your sampling
radius the longer you wait.

With a population size as large as you mention, I wonder if distance
sampling is the appropriate tool for the job?

> > I am currently working on fruit bat surveys at known roosting sites using point counts.
> > The particular site I am working on is small (<3 hectares) and is surrounded by non habitat (water and housing). The population within this area is enormous with over 10,000 roosting at any given time.
> > The counts just completed were undertaken by walking the boundary of bat colony and from certain points (somewhat random) recording all bats seen, and also recording the field of view (usually 180 degrees). Six point counts were undertaken.
> >
> > I analysed the data by treating sample effort as a fraction of 1. i.e 180 degrees is 0.5, and 90 degrees is 0.25. A 360 field of view is required to be 1. I did not use the sampling fraction option as fraction varied between points.
> > Bats are generally not seen beyond 50m, with an ESW of 30m. Interesting detections show a logistic type curve (hazard cosine), increasing from 0, peaking at 15m, and declining to close to 0 by 30m. That may indicate bats moved away from the observer, but Distance is robust (?) I think to this provided animals move no more than detection shoulder (i.e 15-20m)
> > I had some issues with all points being a fraction of 360 degrees and that all points occurred on outside of colony looking in. But perhaps there is no issue there?
> >
> > My idea would be to establish random points within all potential habitats and each point surveyed each year for bats regardless of bats being there. This would inflate estimate of variance however. Points on edge of habitat may be only 180 degrees but most points are 360 as points lie inside colony.
> > Just wondered what others thought.

> > Cheers
